forces: Tenor soloist, mixed chorus, brass, timpani, harp and organ
performers: Michel Sénéchal, tenor; J. J. Grunenwald, organ; Chorale Élisabeth Brasseur; members of the Orchestre des Concerts Lamoureux; Igor Markevitch, conductor
intro: Trumpets, trombones and organ launch Boulanger’s Psalm 24 with a fanfare of bare fifths. Michel Sénéchal’s quiet tenor solo is the still centre of this short, blazing score.

sections.label: A · Brass and lower voices
sections.mNote: Trumpets and trombones answer the tenors and basses

sections.label: B · Tenor with muted horns
sections.mNote: Harp and organ repeat a figure beneath the solo

sections.label: C · The full choir proclaims
sections.mNote: Sopranos and altos join the returning brass fanfares

cues.title: Bare fifths in brass
cues.text: Trumpets and trombones sound the fanfare in bare fifths, with the organ doubling them. Tenors and basses take up the words between the brass replies. Boulanger asks for Vif et décidé — lively and decisive — and gives every syllable a firm edge.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, plate D. & F. 10488 (1924), pp. 1–2; Helen Julia Minors discusses the opening E–B fifths in her 2011 preface. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP306314-PMLP430957-psalm_24_lili_boulanger_4.pdf https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1146.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rome, during the war
cues.text: In 1916 Boulanger is back at the Villa Medici in Rome, where the Prix de Rome has brought her to compose. She writes this psalm and Psalm 129 during the same stay. At the foot of the final page she puts the place and year: Rome, 1916.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1924), p. 18, dated Rome 1916; Helen Julia Minors, preface (2011), gives the circumstances of composition. https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1146.html

cues.title: A blessing, softly
cues.text: The tenor sings of receiving the Lord’s blessing. The horns are muted and play in answering pairs; harp and organ repeat their small figure underneath. The tempo eases, and the solo voice is marked grave et doux — solemn and gentle.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1924), p. 6, figure 3: Un peu moins vite, solo tenor, muted horns, harp ostinato and organ pedal.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A fanfare ensemble, with harps
cues.text: Instead of an orchestra, Boulanger sets the psalm for four-part choir, organ, four horns, three trumpets, four trombones, tuba, timpani and two harps. Apart from the harps, the line-up recalls a fanfare band. The score is dedicated to Jules Griset, director of the Guillot de Saint-Brice choir.
cues.evidence: Helen Julia Minors, preface to Psalm 24 (2011): scoring and dedication. https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1146.html

cues.title: The gates open
cues.text: The full choir calls for the gates to open to the King of Glory. Sopranos and altos now join the lower voices, and the brass fanfares return. Later, trombones, horns and trumpets enter one after another, crowding the same fanfare into overlapping calls.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1924), pp. 8–9, Au mouvement and full-choir entry; subsequent overlapping brass entries discussed in Helen Julia Minors’s preface. https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1146.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nadia at the playback
cues.text: At the Salle Pleyel in Paris, Nadia Boulanger listens to the recorded playbacks of her sister’s music. The album sleeve catches her there in a photograph. She supervises the recording; her former pupil Igor Markevitch conducts.
cues.evidence: Everest LPBR 6059 sleeve (1960): photograph caption, recording-supervision credit and Markevitch biography. https://archive.org/download/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d_djvu.txt

transitions.title: Muted horns around the tenor
transitions.how: The trumpets and trombones fall silent. At Un peu moins vite, the organ holds the bass while harp and muted horns repeat a small figure. The horns answer in pairs. Over this quiet accompaniment the tenor begins his blessing, marked grave et doux.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score (1924), pp. 5–7, figure 3: solo tenor, muted horns in pairs, repeated harp figure and sustained organ bass.

transitions.title: All four voices together
transitions.how: The lower voices stretch their last syllable over moving harp notes and held organ chords. Brass joins the sustained harmony, then the accompaniment stops. At Au mouvement the whole choir begins together, marked éclatant, before the brass answers with the opening fanfare.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score (1924), pp. 8–9: ritardando over the lower voices, held brass and organ chords, then the unaccompanied full-choir entry at Au mouvement.

source.title: Lili Boulanger, Psaume 24, Durand full score (1924), plate D. & F. 10488
source.locator: Instrument list and printed pp. 1, 4–9, 17–18. The score calls for brass, timpani, one harp and organ. Horns can double the lower choir in the opening pages.

timeline.note: Trumpets and trombones proclaim the opening fifths over tuba and organ.
Tenors and basses answer the fanfare over organ and timpani.
Tenors and basses ask who may enter the holy place. Brass chords and harp notes support them.
The tenor sings with muted horns, harp and organ at figure 3.
At Plus lent, part of the lower choir joins the solo tenor over harp and organ.
The full choir proclaims the opening of the gates. Brass fanfares answer its phrases.
The choir holds its final vowel over brass, timpani, harp and organ.

fields.note: Boulanger died in 1918. This is a territorial term calculation for the original music, not a worldwide clearance or a claim about an unidentified modern edition. The biblical or liturgical text is not used as evidence for the sound-recording rights.

The rule concerns first lawful publication anywhere, not first EU publication. On the former fifty-year term this phonogram was no longer protected before the 2013 extension. US recording status is not established. No worldwide public-domain claim, Creative Commons licence or modern-remaster release is inferred.

composer.epithet: At nineteen she won the Prix de Rome; before her death at twenty-four she had written songs of lost love and psalms that shake the room.
facts: Ernest and Raïssa Boulanger’s younger daughter; Nadia’s sister
Paul Vidal for composition; Georges Caussade for counterpoint; Nadia at home
First woman to win the Premier Grand Prix de Rome in composition, 1913
Songs, psalms, chamber and orchestral music; unfinished opera La Princesse Maleine
composer.background:
At the Château de Compiègne in May 1913, five young composers were shut away writing a cantata about Faust and Helen of Troy. Someone had sent champagne. Their joint letter of thanks to the composer Fernand Halphen, dated 31 May and written out by Claude Delvincourt, called them “your young colleagues imprisoned in the château to sing the loves of Faust and Helen”. Among the signatures was Lili Boulanger’s. She was nineteen, and this was her second attempt at the Prix de Rome. Illness had forced her to withdraw the previous year.

In July she became the first woman to win the Premier Grand Prix for musical composition. Thirty-one of the Académie des Beaux-Arts’ thirty-six voters supported her. Faust et Hélène gave them a tenor in love with a woman summoned from antiquity, a mezzo-soprano Helen and a baritone devil, all carried by a substantial orchestra. The compulsory text was Eugène Adenis’s adaptation of Goethe. Lili dedicated the score to Nadia, who had won a second prize in 1908.
